IV. ALTERNATIVES
In recent years, the work of planning for roadway improvements in the Chicago Region has been undertaken by the Chicago Area Transportation Study (C.A.T.S.), by the Department of Transportation (formerly the Illinois Division of Highways) and by the local agencies. The extensive work of the study, commencing in 1956, saw the completion of an improvement plan for the region in 1962.
In 1957, the Illinois General Assembly established the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission (N.I.P.C.) to develop and review plans for all future land use. The primary purpose of these two agencies (C.A.T.S. and N.I.P.C.) was to prepare an optimum comprehensive plan of development for the Chicago Metropolitan Region.
On October 21, 1971, the Northeastern Illinois Planning Commission adopted the Interim Transportation Plan and Program as one of its functional plans. (See Exhibit "5".)
The Illinois Department of Transportation in order to ensure full and continuous community participation in the selection of a highway route generally requires two stages, namely: the Corridor Stage and Design Stage. Employing this technique provides the department the necessary information for decision making. Both the corridor and design stage are developed and analyzed on the following issues:
.....Impact on existing and future social-economic and natural environmental issues.
.....Comprehensive regional and local land use plans.
..... Existing and projected traffic demands.
.....Transportation and related engineering considerations.
The Corridor is generally defined as approximately three (3) miles wide centered on the approximate line as indicated in the Interim Transportation Plan and Program. The demand for a transportation facility is established through the general planning process predicted upon future land use and population. However, the "Three C" planning process has not carried the intent of the plan to the affected individual. The corridor stage is the department's medium for conveying the data evaluated within the approximate three (3) mile corridor and solicitation of other pertinent people values through the public meeting and hearing process.
